about: Every department’s starting budget from FY2010 to FY2025, against the levy and against the schools — and what “deficit” can and cannot mean in this ledger.

conclusions.basis: Finance Committee general fund history, ORIGINAL budget by account; our grouping, stated on the page.
conclusions.claim: Town departments’ starting budgets grew 5.4% a year; the schools’ grew 3.6%.
conclusions.detail: Measured on each year’s ORIGINAL budget, budget to budget. Stopping a year earlier, before the FY2025 override, the gap is wider: town 5.4%, schools 3.1%. With the school’s own health insurance left in, as the ledger books it, the schools grew 3.7%.
conclusions.not_shown: A budget line is net: grants, circuit breaker and fees pay school costs this ledger never sees, so slower appropriation growth is not slower cost growth. Nor is it need.
conclusions.so_what: FY2010 to FY2025, with health insurance taken out of both so they are measured alike.

conclusions.basis: Original budgets as above; DLS certified levy limits and the DLS override register.
conclusions.claim: Ranked by pull on the levy, town departments lead at +0.23 points a year.
conclusions.detail: Pull is each group’s FY2010 share of the budget times how far its growth ran above the levy limit’s, so it weighs size and speed together. The levy benchmark has the voted override taken back out — our choice, so it measures what the levy grows by without a vote.

lx.unit: a year, levy limit less overrides

pt.unit: a year of pull, town departments

conclusions.not_shown: The levy is not all revenue: state aid and local receipts pay part of every line. Debt is partly paid outside the limit by exclusions.
conclusions.so_what: The schools sit at −0.30 points: their starting budget grew slower than the levy limit’s 4.3%.

conclusions.claim: The county retirement assessment grew 9.7% a year — the fastest of any group.
conclusions.detail: From $528,137 in FY2010 to $2,127,801 in FY2025. It sits on the town’s side of the ledger, so a school-versus-town comparison that leaves it there flatters the schools by whatever their share of it is.
conclusions.not_shown: The school share. Teachers are in the state’s system, not this one; every other school employee who is a member is in it, unsplit.
conclusions.so_what: It pays pensions for town and school members alike, and nothing published splits it.

conclusions.basis: REVISED budget against ACTUAL, summed by group, complete years only.
conclusions.claim: The schools spent 98.5% of their final budgets, FY2010 to FY2024; town departments 93.7%.
conclusions.detail: Over the fifteen complete years the town departments left $7,540,321 unspent and the schools $3,685,956. FY2025 is excluded because its actual is part-year.
conclusions.not_shown: Why. Unspent money can be a vacancy, a cautious estimate or a deferred purchase; the ledger records the dollars, not the reason.
conclusions.so_what: No school or town department ended a year over budget except snow removal, once.

conclusions.basis: Department 423, original against actual; transfers in and out.
conclusions.claim: Snow Removal spent above its starting budget in 15 of 15 years.
conclusions.detail: Over the same years $2,075,219 was moved into it by transfer, net. Massachusetts General Laws chapter 44, section 31D allows snow and ice spending past the appropriation if the appropriation is at least the prior year’s.
conclusions.not_shown: Whether the starting figure is set low on purpose. That is how the statute is commonly used, and nothing here tests it.
conclusions.so_what: It is the one budget state law lets run over; transfers then cover it.

conclusions.basis: Revised minus original minus both transfer columns, by account and year.
conclusions.claim: $5,638,195 reached departments’ budgets mid-year with no transfer recorded for it.
conclusions.detail: On 858 account-years the revised budget exceeds original plus transfers. For 75% of those dollars the same account had at least that much unspent the year before, which is what a carried-forward encumbrance would look like. The rest fits a supplemental appropriation.

a.unit: added outside recorded transfers, FY2010 to FY2025

f.unit: of it within the prior year’s unspent

conclusions.not_shown: What any of it was. The ledger prints the revised figure, not the vote or the carry-forward behind it.
conclusions.so_what: 75% of it fits money carried forward from the year before. That is a hypothesis.

conclusions.basis: DLS override register; Finance Committee minutes, 12 February 2026; Select Board minutes, 16 March 2026.
conclusions.claim: The $3,300,000 override voted in 2026 was for town and school budgets alike.
conclusions.detail: Voted 2026-05-16 and lost, as was a second question for $2,400,000; DLS records the larger as “Fund Budgets Town And School For Fy27”. That February the Town Manager asked department heads for a level service budget, and the Select Board then worked a balanced and an unbalanced budget department by department. The ledger itself holds no request or level-service column for any year, so a “deficit” is need minus revenue and need is not in it.
literals: Fund Budgets Town And School For Fy27
conclusions.not_shown: Whether the town’s departments would have shown a gap in earlier years if priced the same way. Their past requests to the Town Manager would settle it.
conclusions.so_what: In a year the town priced level service, the ask covered its own departments too.

grain: DOLLARS of general fund appropriation. Growth is the ORIGINAL budget, budget to budget; spending is the REVISED budget against ACTUAL, FY2010 to FY2024 only. Groups, the benchmark and the treatment of health insurance are ours.

What the money that reached revised budgets outside any recorded transfer was.
The school share of the county retirement assessment, of Medicare, and of retirees’ health insurance before the ledger split it.
How much of the schools’ appropriation growth is cost growth and how much is grants, circuit breaker or fees starting or stopping.
